name: Ohel (Tent) as Vehicle of Corpse Impurity
notes: Detailed laws of how a tent/covering spreads or blocks corpse impurity, including minimum sizes, slopes, partial coverings, and configurations of structures

name: Minimum Quantities for Corpse Impurity (Shiurei Tumat Met)
notes: Specific minimum quantities that convey corpse impurity: olive-size of flesh, quarter-kav of bones, quarter-log of blood, ladleful of corpse mold, etc.

name: Nezel (Corpse Fluid)
notes: The fluid that drains from a decomposing corpse and its role in transmitting impurity

name: Afar Kuvarim (Grave Dust / Corpse Mold)
notes: Dust or mold from a decomposed corpse and its minimum quantity (ladleful) for conveying impurity

name: Dam HaMet (Blood of a Corpse)
notes: Blood of a corpse that conveys impurity, including mixed blood (dam tarbut), minimum quantity of quarter-log, and distinctions between blood that flowed during life vs. after death

name: Limbs from a Corpse (Evarim min HaMet)
notes: Laws of whole limbs severed from a corpse or from a living person and how they convey impurity; the 248 limbs of the human body and their required flesh content

name: Spreading and Blocking of Corpse Impurity (Mevi and Chotzetz)
notes: Objects and structures that spread (mevi) corpse impurity to other spaces vs. those that block (chotzetz) its transmission; requires one cubic handbreadth space

name: One Cubic Handbreadth (Tefach Murbah) as Threshold for Impurity
notes: The minimum space of one cubic handbreadth (tefach al tefach b'rum tefach) that constitutes a halakhic 'tent' for purposes of corpse impurity

name: Sealed Vessel Protecting Contents in Ohel (Tzamid Patil b'Ohel)
notes: Earthenware vessel sealed with a tight-fitting lid protecting its contents from corpse impurity inside a tent; dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel

name: Bet HaPeras (Field with Plowed Grave)
notes: Detailed laws of a field made impure by plowing over a grave, its dimensions (100 cubits furrow), types (plowed grave, lost grave, kokhin field), purification methods, and examination procedures

name: Field in Which a Grave Was Lost (Sadeh sheNiavad Kever)
notes: A field in which a grave has been lost, distinguished from a plowed-over grave field; may be sown but not planted, transmits impurity by overshadowing

name: Kokhin Field (Sadeh Kokhin)
notes: A field used for burial niches (kokhin); may neither be planted nor sown, but its earth is considered clean for use in making ovens for sacred purposes

name: Impurity of the Land of the Nations (Tumat Eretz HaAmim)
notes: Rabbinic decree that lands of non-Jews convey impurity; detailed rules about travel over such lands, purchasing fields in Syria, and how this interacts with terumah and shemitah obligations

name: Impurity of Non-Jewish Dwellings (Tumat Ohel Nochrim)
notes: Rabbinic decree that dwellings of non-Jews are impure due to presumption that fetuses were buried beneath them; requires examination after 40 days of habitation

name: Finding Multiple Corpses and Establishing a Graveyard
notes: Laws governing discovery of corpses in a field: finding one may be removed, finding three within a space of a bier and bearers (4-8 cubits) establishes a graveyard requiring 20-cubit search

name: Opening of the Grave/Womb (Pesicat HaKever)
notes: The concept of the womb opening during childbirth creating impurity like a grave opening; stillborn children and the point at which the womb is considered 'opened'

name: Impurity Goes Out but Does Not Go In (Darkah Latzet v'Lo Lavo)
notes: Halakhic principle that corpse impurity naturally spreads outward from its source, so a sealed inner space may protect against outside impurity but not against impurity within it

name: Garlic Skin Principle (Klipat HaShum)
notes: A covering as thin as garlic skin can block corpse impurity if there is a space of one cubic handbreadth beneath it; used in cases of covering over drains, pillars, and wall spaces

name: Objects That Convey vs. Block Impurity (Mevi u'Chotzetz)
notes: Classification of objects into: those that both convey and block impurity, those that convey but don't block, those that block but don't convey, and those that neither convey nor block

name: Chain of Defilement from Corpse (Shelshelel HaTumah)
notes: The graduated chain of corpse impurity transmission: first-degree (corpse itself), persons and vessels touching it receive 7-day impurity, subsequent generations receive evening-only impurity; the maximum chain length

name: Bone the Size of a Barleycorn (Etzem k'Seorah)
notes: Minimum bone fragment (barleycorn size) that conveys corpse impurity by contact and carrying but not by overshadowing; disputes about divided bones

name: Majority or Structural Majority of a Corpse's Bones
hebrew: רוב בניינו ורוב מניינו של מת
notes: The structural majority (rov binyan) or numerical majority (rov minyan, 125 bones) of a corpse's skeleton that conveys full corpse impurity including by overshadowing

name: Minimum Opening Size for Impurity Passage (Shiur Petach HaOhel)
notes: Detailed rules about minimum opening sizes (one handbreadth square, or drill-hole size) in walls, doors, windows, and ceilings that allow corpse impurity to pass through or that protect against its spread

name: Form of a Doorway (Tzurat HaPetach) in Impurity Context
notes: In Oholot, the intended use of an opening (for a door, light, ventilation, etc.) determines its minimum size threshold for conveying or blocking impurity

name: 248 Limbs of the Human Body
notes: The enumeration of 248 limbs in the human body; each whole limb with appropriate flesh can defile by contact, carrying, and overshadowing

name: Covering Stone and Buttressing Stone of a Grave
notes: The flat stone covering a burial niche and the stone supporting it; they defile by contact and overshadowing; dispute whether they defile by carrying and whether grave dust beneath them matters

name: Projections and Balconies as Ohel (Ziz and Gessissah)
notes: Architectural projections (ziz), balconies (gessissah), and cornices extending from a wall that serve as ohel for transmitting or blocking corpse impurity; minimum width of one handbreadth

name: Tent Made by Human Action vs. Naturally Formed Tent
notes: Dispute (Rabbi Judah) whether a tent must be deliberately made by a human to qualify as a halakhic ohel, or whether naturally formed enclosures (crevices, crags) also qualify

name: Persons and Vessels as Ohel (Adam u'Kelim k'Ohel)
notes: Living persons and vessels can serve as an ohel to convey corpse impurity (e.g., pallbearers carrying a coffin) but cannot serve as an ohel to protect against impurity
